query: Why do some incidents take longer to resolve?

per_column.name: incident_category
per_column.rationale: Categorizing incidents (vpn, database, email, network) gives a strong axis to compare resolution times across incident types. Values are well-grounded in short_description text; partly overlaps existing 'category' but the finer granularity adds leverage.

per_column.name: failure_pattern
per_column.rationale: Failure mode (connection_failure, service_down, sync_crash) is a genuine new grouping axis relevant to why some incidents take longer. Values are reasonable readings of descriptions, though some ('service_down' for 'Email system not working properly') are mild inferences.

per_column.name: scope_indicator
per_column.rationale: Scope (individual vs department-wide vs outage) is highly relevant to resolution effort. However some values overreach: 'WiFi connectivity issue in the sales department' -> department_wide is warranted, but many outage_wide/production_environment labels are not clearly supported by terse descriptions, and 'VPN connection issue' -> individual_user is a guess where text is silent on scope.

per_column.name: assignment_lag
per_column.rationale: Time-to-assignment is directly relevant to resolution duration. But grounding is questionable: the samples show only sys_updated_on and closed_at (equal), with no opened_at/assignment timestamp shown; e.g. same-timestamp rows are labeled 'same_day', 'next_day', and 'multi_day' inconsistently, suggesting values may not be soundly derived from available time fields.

per_column.name: assignee_workload_signal
per_column.rationale: Assignee workload is a plausible driver of delay and can be derived by aggregating assigned_to counts. The high/low binning is a defensible computed signal, though the threshold is opaque; 'unassigned' aligns with missing assignee.

per_column.name: reassignment_indicator
per_column.rationale: Reassignment (ticket bouncing) is relevant to longer resolution. But the table exposes no assignment history; with only one assigned_to and assignment_group column, a per-row true/false reassignment flag is not soundly derivable and appears asserted (290 true) without supporting evidence.

per_column.name: remote_context
per_column.rationale: A remote/VPN context flag is somewhat useful but largely a restatement derivable from incident_category (vpn/network). Values are reasonably grounded in description text (VPN=true).

per_column.name: caller_repeat_reporter
per_column.rationale: Near-constant (all 500 = true), providing zero discriminating power for analysis. It also asserts every caller is a repeat reporter, which cannot be validated from the shown single-incident rows and is likely an unsupported blanket claim.

per_column.name: incident_is_open_unresolved
per_column.rationale: Open/unresolved status is relevant (open tickets are by definition slower), derivable from state/closed_at. Somewhat redundant with existing 'state', but the boolean is a convenient analytical axis and grounded.

judge.rationale: Most added columns (incident_category, failure_pattern, scope_indicator, assignee_workload_signal, incident_is_open_unresolved) provide genuine new axes to explain resolution-time variation and are largely grounded in the description and status fields. However, several columns show grounding weaknesses: assignment_lag appears inconsistently derived from the available timestamps, reassignment_indicator asserts history the table does not expose, and caller_repeat_reporter is both near-constant (no analytical value) and an unsupported blanket true. Overall the set is useful for the query but carries meaningful hallucination risk in the temporal/history-derived flags.
